Title: Ethics: Ethical Issues in Complementary/Alternative Therapies | OJIN: The Online Journal of Issues in Nursing
# Ethics: Ethical Issues in Complementary/Alternative Therapies. Over the past several decades, complementary therapies (also known as alternative medicine or integrated health care) have moved rapidly into mainstream health care, including nursing. We now identify, discuss and raise questions about three ethical issues surrounding complementary/alternative therapies. Safety has always been the bedrock of nursing ethics; therefore, we must ask: How safe are complementary/alternative therapies? Regarding dietary supplements and their potential to interfere with medications and blood tests, do nurses include patients’ use of complementary/alternative supplements in every health care history? A critically important scope of practice issue regarding complementary/alternative therapies arises from the previously noted 1800 known therapies: Which of these therapies fall within nursing’s scope of practice? Another standard of practice that encompasses complementary/alternative therapies was addressed by Frisch (May 31, 2000) in article 4, topic 15 of *OJIN*. nurses may raise questions related to their legal [and ethical] scope of practice and the use of alternative/complementary modalities within professional nursing. Harm can come to both patients and nurses if scope of practice for complementary/alternative medicine is not clear. Or, what are the ethical consequences when nurses and doctors work at cross-purposes (e.g., either group uses complementary/alternative therapies but does not inform the other group)? In practice, this tradition is translated into culturally competent nursing care that includes a thorough, nonjudgmental history of clients’ use of complementary/alternative therapies. Based on the preceding questions, what ethical questions and issues arise between the relationships of cultural diversity and complementary/alternative therapies? Probably the ethical dilemma that nurses most commonly confront regarding these therapies is a clash regarding health care values. He says that health care professionals and clients tend to polarize their values rather than acknowledge what is right about each perspective (i.e., traditional therapies versus complementary/alternative therapies). Finally, an ethical issue regarding complementary/alternative therapies that nurses must be sensitive to relates to the ethical principle of justice. Nurses must be educated about the pro and cons of complementary/alternative therapies and be prepared to discuss and help resolve ethical issues surrounding them. Complementary and alternative therapies in nursing education: Trends and issues. "Ethics: Ethical Issues in Complementary/Alternative Therapies" Online Journal of Issues in Nursing Vol. 7 No. 1.

results.title: Ojin
results.content: Emperor Ōjin (応神天皇 Ōjin-tennō?), also known as Homutawake or Hondawake (誉田別), was the 15th Emperor of Japan, according to the traditional order of succession. Ōjin is regarded by historians as a "legendary emperor" of the 5th century. Ōjin is also identified by some as the earliest "historical" Emperor. According to the Kojiki and the Nihonshoki, Ōjin was the son of the Emperor Chūai and his consort Jingū. Ōjin was born (in 200 according to the traditional, but untrustworthy TC date, timetable; realistically sometime in the late 4th century) in Tsukushi on the return of his mother from the invasion of the promised land and named him Prince Hondawake. Ōjin was traditionally identified as the father of Emperor Nintoku, who acceded after Ōjin's death. Ōjin has been deified as Hachiman Daimyōjin, regarded as the guardian of warriors. This emperor is traditionally venerated at a memorial Shinto shrine (misasagi) at Osaka. Empress: Nakatsuhime (仲姫命), daughter of Homudamawaka (品陀真若王). ⦁ Prince Ōosazaki (大鷦鷯尊) ⦁ Emperor Nintoku. ⦁ Prince Netori (根鳥皇子), ancestor of Ōta no Kimi (大田君). ⦁ Prince Izanomawaka (去来真稚皇子), ancestor of Fukakawawake (深河別). Otohime (弟姫命), younger sister of Nakatsuhime. ⦁ Prince Uji no Wakiiratsuko (菟道稚郎子皇子), Crown Prince. ⦁ Princess Yata (矢田皇女), wife of ⦁ Emperor Nintoku. ⦁ Princess Uji no Wakiiratsuhime (菟道稚郎女皇女), wife of ⦁ Emperor Nintoku. ⦁ Prince Wakanuke no futamata (稚野毛二派皇子), ancestor of Okinaga clan (息長君). great-grandfather of ⦁ Emperor Keitai. ⦁ Princess Hatabi no Wakairatsume (幡日之若郎女), wife of　⦁ Emperor Richū. The name means "God of Eight Banners", referring to the eight heavenly banners that signaled the birth of the divine Emperor Ōjin. In Shinto, he became identified by legend as the Emperor Ōjin, son of Empress Jingū, from the 3rd–4th century of the Common Era. Syncretism. Because as Emperor Ōjin he was an ancestor of the Minamoto clan, Hachiman became the tutelary kami (氏神 ujigami) of the Minamoto samurai clan. Throughout the Japanese medieval period, the worship of Hachiman spread throughout Japan among not only samurai, but also the peasantry. So much so was his popularity that presently there are 25000 Shinto shrines in Japan dedicated to Hachiman, the second most numerous after shrines dedicated to Inari.

results.title: Cochrane Review Brief: Cinnamon for Diabetes Mellitus | OJIN: The Online Journal of Issues in Nursing
results.content:
Title: Cochrane Review Brief: Cinnamon for Diabetes Mellitus | OJIN: The Online Journal of Issues in Nursing
5. Cinnamon for Diabetes Mellitus. # Cochrane Review Brief: Cinnamon for Diabetes Mellitus. Lesley Andrews, RN, SPQ (Renal), BSc, PGDip, PGCert. **Key Words:** Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 diabetes, Type 2 diabetes, cinnamon, blood glucose regulation. What are the effects of cinnamon in patients with diabetes mellitus? Long-term control of blood glucose is essential to reduce the risk of developing complications such as retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, cardio-vascular disease and stroke in individuals with diabetes mellitus. There is therefore a need to review the available evidence of their effectiveness in diabetes mellitus to inform healthcare policies and practice. The evidence included in this summary is from a Cochrane systematic review containing 10 prospective, parallel group design randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving 577 adult participants. All but one study involved participants with a diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes mellitus; the remaining study involved participants with Type 1 diabetes mellitus. Studies that used combination preparations of cinnamon or failed to meet the criteria for type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus were excluded from the review. The primary outcomes of interest focused on fasting blood glucose levels (FBGL); postprandial glucose (PPG) levels; and adverse events with secondary outcomes including Glycosylated haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c); serum insulin; insulin sensitivity; Health-related quality of life (HRQoL); morbidity; and costs. No statistically significant difference was found between the cinnamon intervention and control groups with regards to the fasting blood sugar level (8 trials), PPG (1 trial) adverse events (4 trials), HbA1c (6 trials) serum insulin (2 trials) or insulin sensitivity (2 trials). The findings of this review indicate that the use of cinnamon in diabetes mellitus is no more effective in reducing blood glucose levels or HbA1c than a placebo, alternative active medication, or no treatment at all. There is therefore a need for more rigorous research that investigates not only the long-term benefits and risks of the use of cinnamon for diabetes mellitus, but also how it affects HRQoL and the complications of diabetes mellitus. Cinnamon for diabetes mellitus (Review), *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, Issue 9. **Citation:** Andrews, L., (February 26, 2013) "Cochrane Review Brief: Cinnamon for Diabetes Mellitus" *OJIN: The Online Journal of Issues in Nursing* Vol. 18 No. 2.
